extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and scholarly publishing, journal editors, publishers, research funders, and policy-makers interested in research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A broad, interdisciplinary review identifying gaps in theoretical and empirical understanding of peer review, outlining core themes (editors, reviewers, function/quality, social/epistemic impacts, innovations) and recommending data, standards and research priorities for Peer Review Studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors wield supreme, executive power in the scholarly publishing decision-making process and justifications or criteria for editorial rejections (desk or post-review) are rarely given or automated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should provide the name of the handling editor and other editorial staff, disclose previous interactions with reviewers/authors, and make clear the depth of evaluation applied to a manuscript; but must be mindful this could lead to status-based judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of editors' conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often fail to disclose their conflicts of interest, which can compromise objectivity and influence decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should declare individual conflicts of interest and journals/publishers should have policies and data to enable inspection of how such conflicts relate to editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and sharing of peer review workflow data (including referee recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is limited sharing of data on peer review workflows and referee recommendations; understanding the relationship between recommendations and editorial decisions requires access to these data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and publishers should share workflow data (where possible) to enable analysis of editorial decisions, improve systems, and inform training; beware of private 'file-drawer' internal analyses that are not published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and desk-rejection practices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is rarely explicitly known whether journals send all submissions out for peer review or selectively desk-reject based on scope/fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report proportions of desk rejections versus rejections after peer review to clarify editorial triage practices and their implications for authors and the publication system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rates and prior-rejection history
rubrics_metrics.description: There is patchy insight into the number of times a paper might have been rejected before final acceptance and acceptance-rate statistics across journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and publish acceptance rates and, where possible, histories of prior submissions to understand selection pressures and cascades between journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor practices for signalling reviewer priority
rubrics_metrics.description: How editors signal to authors which reviewer comments are more important (and which can be overlooked) is unclear and affects author responses and manuscript revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should clarify which reviewer points are mandatory versus optional and provide transparency about how they weight reviewer input in decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial assignment practices and potential manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether editors assign particular reviewers to generate a specific desired outcome is currently unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and audit reviewer assignment patterns to detect gaming or bias; journals should document rationale for reviewer selection where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer impartiality and bias (demographic and non-demographic factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer impartiality is affected by author nationality, institutional prestige, reviewer nationality, gender, confirmation and publication bias, personal relationships, workload pressures, emotional state, cognitive style, and other hidden social dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies should measure how these factors influence review decisions and consider policies (blinding, training, diversity in reviewer pools) to mitigate biases; capture data beyond published samples to understand system-level biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'peer' and assessment of reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes a 'peer' and 'expertise' is multi-dimensional and varies by discipline, career stage, research history and over time; factors that prescribe these concepts are often concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop operationalizable indicators of reviewer expertise for different disciplines and examine whether reviewing skills improve over time and across journal types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying reviewer roles and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are often expected to perform inconsistent and multiple tasks (providing recommendations, addressing ethical concerns, assessing content, making general comments) but expectations vary widely between publishers/journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should provide absolute clarity regarding reviewer roles, the expected tasks (e.g., methods/statistics checks, replication attempts), and compliance should be monitored and reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding vs open identities (open peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists whether blinding offers protection or whether openness increases accountability; open identities may deter early-career reviewers or reduce irresponsible behaviour but may also expose social structures that perpetuate bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine empirically (across fields) effects of identity openness on reviewer acceptance rates, report quality, length, timeliness, recommendations, and potential reprisals; consider hybrid or context-dependent models and safeguards for vulnerable reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing review reports (transparency of reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing review reports could increase transparency, but may change reviewers' behaviour (either making them more constructive or more lenient) and will be skewed toward ultimately published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how making reports public affects reviewer willingness, tone, detail, submission time, costs, and the representativeness of the resulting public record; consider whether editorial comments should be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review functionality and definition of review 'quality'
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a lack of consensus about what peer review is for and what differentiates a 'good' review from a 'bad' one; review quality may relate to methodological interrogation, error detection, speed, or strengthening argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop clear, possibly discipline-specific definitions and operational metrics for review quality; research should distinguish between 'value' (subjective impact) and 'quality' (process rigour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process metrics (operational data to measure peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of empirical elements that could be gathered to understand peer review functionality (duration of phases, number of reports per article, length of reports, number of rounds, availability and inspection of code/data, reviewer decline rates, acceptance rates, who decides openness, desk rejection proportions, ultimate fate of manuscripts, whether the reviewing journal was the reviewer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect standardized, longitudinal data on these metrics across journals/publishers/disciplines to enable systematic comparison and evaluation of peer review function and cost/time trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection/use of code, data and materials during review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether code, data and materials are made available during review and whether these are inspected/analysed during the process is rarely known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should require or encourage availability of materials and document whether and how reviewers (or editorial staff) inspected them; consider incentives or support for reviewers to perform such checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialised reviewers and reproducibility testing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unknown whether specialised reviewers (methods/statistics) are used and whether they apply skills to test the rigour of research; reproducibility of peer review (e.g., inter-reviewer reliability) shows variable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate using specialist reviewers systematically, test inter-reviewer reliability, and evaluate whether including specialists improves detection of errors and reproducibility of review outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of automated tools and services in review
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated services (statistical checks, plagiarism detection, reviewer-locators) are starting to be used, but their role, effect on reviewer selection, workload, and on peer review quality is poorly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cost, effectiveness and consequences of automated tools and whether automation mitigates or introduces biases; examine effects on time-to-decision and reviewer labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives, recognition and workload for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general lack of rewards/incentives for reviewers which undermines rigorous testing; some journals offer credits or discounts but the attractiveness and impact are unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study incentive schemes (credits, discounts, metrics such as F3-index) for reviewer recruitment and quality, and measure reviewer workload distribution and fatigue effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to enable detection and remediation of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency in reviewer identity and reports may make it easier to inspect relationships, motivations, and address bias or misconduct (e.g., via COPE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish or provide access to sufficient metadata (identities where appropriate, relationships, and review histories) to allow third-party investigation, while balancing protections for vulnerable reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and epistemic impacts of peer review (epistemic diversity and exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review affects the composition of scientific discourse and may contribute to epistemic homogeneity, conservatism, Matthew effects, and unequal diffusion of ideas; the learning benefits to participants are also understudied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically study how peer review influences innovation, epistemic diversity, career outcomes, and post-publication evaluation systems; distinguish intrinsic peer-review biases from larger socio-cultural drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between innovation and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review may suppress innovation through conservatism; it is unclear where the balance between rapid dissemination and slow critical assessment should lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should quantify the dynamic trade-offs between speed, novelty acceptance, and quality assurance, and identify points where peer review becomes redundant or obstructive in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for consensus minimal standards for what constitutes peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The field lacks a consensus for a minimal set of standards for what constitutes peer review, hampering comparative study and policy-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and adopt community-endorsed minimum standards defining peer review elements (e.g., number of reviewers, documentation of decisions, data availability expectations) to enable comparability and build shared infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of shared peer review data infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: A shared data infrastructure is required to support empirical Peer Review Studies, but sustained funding and commitment from publishers and funders are largely absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create interoperable data standards and repositories for anonymized or consented peer review metadata to enable large-scale, reproducible studies and tooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Version tracking and measuring 'value added' of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: There is limited understanding of what changes peer review actually makes between versions (preprints vs final published articles) and whether peer review adds substantive value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement version-control comparisons and measure changes attributable to peer review (style, methods, results interpretation) to evaluate peer review's real impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardised peer review checklists and quality-assessment tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of standardised peer review 'check-lists' could guide reviewers, but research and tools for measuring review quality are in their infancy and often discipline-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop, validate and disseminate checklists and tools (tailored by discipline) to improve consistency and enable measurement of review thoroughness and content focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating reviewer pool concentration and equity of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence suggests a relatively small pool of researchers performs the majority of reviewing, raising questions about exhaustion, selection of 'good' reviewers, and inequities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure distribution of reviewing workload, recruitment practices, and the demographic composition of reviewer pools; design policies to broaden participation and avoid reviewer fatigue.
